newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-HOGAN, ONE OF THE WORLD'S GREATEST GOLFERS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-HOGAN, ONE OF THE WORLD'S GREATEST GOLFERS.

text.p: There are two main schools of thought about Ben Hogan's place in the golfing hall of fame.
One school says Hogan, who died Friday at the age of 84, would have been the greatest in the history of the game if he had not smashed his legs in a near- fatal car crash.
The other argues he was the best, anyway.
Gene Sarazen, who played with many of the top golfers of the century, was once asked to name the best. "It would have to be Ben Hogan," he said..

Hogan's record -- four U.S. Open titles, two Masters, two PGA championships, one British Open -- tells only part of the story. The other part is the dedication that made him a top golfer and the recovery from a terrible car crash.
Stardom did not come easily for Hogan, who was born on August 13, 1912. Unlike Sam Snead and Byron Nelson, two big rivals born in the same year, he did not have a natural swing.
He compensated by spending hours on the practice range, sometimes leaving in tears at his frustration to hit the ball the way he wanted.

After 16 years as a professional he still had a chronic hook and only one major title to his credit. But his practice and dedication paid off when, virtually overnight, he finally struck on a reliable swing.
Hogan became nearly unbeatable, winning 13 events in 1946, seven in 1947 and 11 in 1948, including the U.S. Open at the Riviera club in Los Angeles with a record score of 276.

Just as he was reaching the full height of his game, a bus slammed into his car in west Texas in 1949 while he was driving home with his wife. Hogan's injuries included a fractured pelvis, broken collar-bone, ribs and ankle requiring two months in a hospital and almost a year of convalescence.
At one time it looked as if he would never walk again, let alone play golf. But the sceptics were confounded by Hogan's awesome determination.

The very next year, aged 37, he made his comeback in the Los Angeles Open, and only lost to Snead in a playoff. Then came the U.S. Open at Merion, and to everyone's amazement he opened with 72-69 to trail by just two strokes.
However, the final two rounds were played on the same day in brutal heat, and no one thought Hogan could last.
"Ben just can't do it. Thirty-six holes in one day will kill him," Sarazen predicted.

Hogan did wilt in the final round, even falling down on one tee, but he salvaged par at the last hole to earn a playoff against Lloyd Mangrum and George Fazio. The next day he capped a storybook comeback, winning the crown with a 69.
His heroism captured the imagination of America, and Hollywood quickly came out with "Follow the Sun," a movie dramatising the Hogan story. Glenn Ford played the lead.

Hogan was born on August 3, 1912, the son of an Irish blacksmith in Dublin, Texas. His father committed suicide when Ben was nine, and he began his golfing career with two years as a caddie as a way of bringing in money for the family.

He showed promise as a player and in 1931 tried his luck on the tour. But he found no instant success and made up for his lack of income through occasional work as an oil-field worker, mechanic and bank clerk.
After countless hours of practice came his breakthrough, which he explained the following way in a rare interview.

"One night in bed I got an idea, something I might try. Well, I could barely wait for the sun to come up the next morning. Out I went to the practice tee and started trying out my theory. It worked. It worked all day long. And the next day. And the next day, too."
The alteration cured his chronic hook, and ever after Hogan became famed as a "shotmaker," possessing the ability to hit the ball high or low, with a hook or fade, whenever he wished.
Hogan won 15 tournaments in the 1940-42 seasons, but his career was interrupted by World War II when he served in the Air Corps.
He resumed his winning ways after the war ended and even the car wreck could not stop him. He followed his epic triumph at Merion by retaining the U.S. Open the next year along with the Masters.
The best was yet to come. In 1953, aged 40, Hogan won the Masters by a then-record margin of five strokes, the U.S. Open by six, and crossed the Atlantic for his only British Open.

Fighting a cold wind over the punishing Carnoustie course, Hogan produced a course-record 68 in the final round for victory, and complete a sweep of three wins in all three major championships he entered that season.
Appreciative Scottish golf fans impressed by his tenacity dubbed the diminutive Hogan "Wee Ice Mon," adding to his previous nicknames of "Bantam Ben" and "Hawk."
In later years, as with so many golfers, his putting touch deserted him, and he played his final tournament in 1971.

Hogan then devoted himself to the golf equipment company that bore his name, but was still frequently seen putting in hours of practice at a course near the Fort Worth home where he lived with his wife, Valerie. They had no children.
His book, "Five Lessons: The Modern Fundamentals of Golf," remains a teaching classic that still applies to this day.
Always a solitary person, Hogan became a virtual recluse in retirement, rarely granting interviews.
He even more rarely gave specific advice.
Briton Nick Faldo, whom some say resembles Hogan in his almost obsessive quest for the perfect golf swing, sought out Hogan.
This was before Faldo won his third Masters to add to his three British Open titles.
Faldo finally was granted an audience and asked for the secret to winning.
The famously-taciturn Hogan drawled, "Shoot the lowest score."
